This value reflects the mass of the albumen-buffered embryo shortly after syngamy, prior to the onset of intensive parental incubation. When eggs are maintained at a constant incubation temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the embryonated egg requires approximately 23 days [ab = approximately 23 days] to reach the hatching event. This incubation period is broadly consistent with values reported for other small-bodied psittaciforms, where a trade-off exists between thermal constancy and developmental rate. The dependence of hatching success on precise temperature regulation is well documented, and deviations from this optimal thermal regime can delay emergence or reduce hatchling viability. Upon hatching, the nestling chick emerges with a wet weight at birth of 2.5 grams [Wwb = 2.5 grams], a modest mass that underscores the altricial nature of the hatchling, which is entirely dependent on parental provisioning and brooding for thermoregulation during the first days of life.

This relatively extended nestling period is typical of altricial psittaciformes, which require substantial time for feather maturation and neuromuscular coordination before achieving independence. The attainment of flight is a critical threshold; post-fledging, the young bird remains dependent on parental food deliveries for several additional weeks while it refines its foraging skills. Continued growth during this period allows the fledgling to approach the species' ultimate wet weight of 56 grams [Wwi = 56 grams], a mass that characterizes the sexually mature adult and represents the asymptotic body size of the species.
